title: With Due Respect (Vol. 4) -- Ch. 7: Divorce, Pinoy Style
keywords: Te v. Te and Azcueta v. Republic
primary_topics: Chapter 7 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 4) -- CJP's February 21, 2010 Inquirer column explaining that while Western-style absolute divorce between two Filipinos is invalid here, courts can void a marriage for a fatal defect at its inception, most commonly 'psychological incapacity' under Article 36 of the Family Code

The doctrine's evolution from Santos v. Court of Appeals (1995), which confined psychological incapacity to 'the most serious cases of personality disorders' marked by 'gravity, juridical antecedence and incurability,' to Republic v. Molina (1997), which laid down eight strict guidelines

How the Court later loosened the doctrine -- abandoning Molina's eighth guideline (mandatory solicitor-general participation) in 2003 over CJP's dissent, and adopting a 'case-to-case' approach in Te v. Te and Azcueta (2009) that treats the guidelines as not a 'straightjacket'

CJP's concern that the relaxation has left 'no more firm standards,' making outcomes hard to predict and prompting critics to say the country is 'back to the most liberal divorce procedure in the world' -- the 'Pinoy edition' of absolute divorce
sub_topics: The premise: a Western-style absolute divorce between two Filipinos -- 'even if obtained abroad' -- 'is not valid here,' but courts can void a marriage 'due to a fatal defect at its inception,' most commonly 'psychological incapacity' under Article 36 of the Family Code (effective August 3, 1988), whose 'interpretation and application are still evolving'

The statute: Article 36 voids a marriage where a party was, 'at the time of the celebration,' 'psychologically incapacitated to comply with the essential marital obligations,' even if the incapacity 'becomes manifest only after its solemnization'

The first decision -- Santos v. Court of Appeals (January 4, 1995): psychological incapacity means 'no less than a mental (not physical) incapacity,' confined to 'the most serious cases of personality disorders' showing 'utter insensitivity or inability to give meaning... to the marriage,' and must be marked by 'gravity, juridical antecedence and incurability'
The call for guidelines: judges and lawyers found Santos hard to apply, and the OSG -- calling Article 36 'the most liberal divorce procedure in the world' -- asked the Court to standardize it

Republic v. Molina (February 13, 1997): drawing on Archbishop Oscar Cruz (head of the Church's National Appellate Matrimonial Tribunal) as amicus, the Court issued eight guidelines -- plaintiff's burden of proof (doubts resolved for validity); a root cause medically identified, alleged, expert-proven and explained; incapacity existing 'at the time of the celebration'; incurability; gravity (not mere 'mild characterological peculiarities'); the essential obligations under Family Code Articles 68-71 (and 220, 221, 225); great respect for matrimonial-tribunal interpretations; and mandatory appearance and certification by the prosecutor and solicitor general

Back to liberality: criticized as 'too strict,' the guidelines were loosened when the Court 'abandoned item no. 8 in 2003' -- over CJP's dissent that the OSG's 'active intervention was necessary,' like the Church's 'defensor vinculi' (defender of the bond), to keep the process from 'degenerat[ing] to a divorce fiat'

The case-to-case turn: Te v. Te (February 13, 2009) and Azcueta v. Republic (May 26, 2009) held the guidelines should not be a 'straightjacket' and, 'while not suggesting the abandonment of Molina,' said courts should decide 'on a case-to-case basis, guided by experience, the findings of experts... and... church tribunals'

The upshot: with 'no more firm standards,' outcomes are 'difficult to predict,' defective judgments often go unappealed (the OSG no longer mandated to defend the bond), and critics say the country is 'back to the most liberal divorce procedure in the world' -- the 'Pinoy edition' of absolute divorce

stances.claim: The Philippines has no absolute divorce, but Article 36's 'psychological incapacity' lets courts void a marriage for a fatal defect at its inception -- a doctrine whose 'interpretation and application are still evolving' from the strict Santos and Molina standards toward greater liberality.
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal-explainer: tracing how a single statutory phrase has been judicially defined and redefined
stances.confidence: asserted as the state of the law

stances.claim: Loosening Molina was a mistake in one key respect: CJP dissented from abandoning the mandatory solicitor-general role in 2003, arguing the OSG's 'active intervention was necessary' -- like the Church's 'defensor vinculi' -- to keep nullity from 'degenerat[ing] to a divorce fiat.'
stances.rhetorical_move: recorded-dissent: flagging his own contrary view on a specific relaxation of the rules

stances.claim: The 'case-to-case' turn in Te and Azcueta has left 'no more firm standards,' making outcomes unpredictable and defective judgments often unappealed -- so critics now call it 'the most liberal divorce procedure in the world,' the 'Pinoy edition' of absolute divorce.
stances.rhetorical_move: consequence-assessment: reading the doctrinal drift as a slide back toward de facto divorce

notable_anecdotes: Divorce by another name: CJP opens by noting that absolute divorce between Filipinos is invalid here, yet 'psychological incapacity' under Article 36 functions as a Filipino route to ending a marriage.
The OSG's barb: he relays the Solicitor General's exaggeration that Article 36 was 'the most liberal divorce procedure in the world,' the spur for the Molina guidelines.

The archbishop as amicus: he recounts the Court inviting Archbishop Oscar Cruz, head of the Church's matrimonial tribunal, to explain Article 36's Canon-Law roots before issuing the eight Molina guidelines.

His own dissent: he notes dissenting when the Court dropped the mandatory OSG role in 2003, invoking the Church's 'defensor vinculi' to argue the state must oppose nullity petitions lest the process become 'a divorce fiat.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 7 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 4), CJP's February 21, 2010 Inquirer column, explains that while a Western-style absolute divorce between two Filipinos 'is not valid here,' courts can void a marriage for 'a fatal defect at its inception' -- most commonly 'psychological incapacity' under Article 36 of the Family Code (effective August 3, 1988), a doctrine 'still evolving.' Article 36 voids a marriage where a party was, 'at the time of the celebration,' incapable of complying with 'the essential marital obligations,' even if the incapacity surfaces later. The first ruling, Santos v. Court of Appeals (1995), confined it to 'the most serious cases of personality disorders' marked by 'gravity, juridical antecedence and incurability'; but because judges struggled to apply it -- and the OSG branded Article 36 'the most liberal divorce procedure in the world' -- the Court, drawing on Archbishop Oscar Cruz as amicus, issued eight strict guidelines in Republic v. Molina (1997), covering the plaintiff's burden, a medically identified and proven root cause, incapacity at the time of celebration, incurability, gravity, the essential obligations under the Family Code, respect for church-tribunal interpretations, and mandatory solicitor-general participation. Criticized as 'too strict,' the guidelines were loosened: the Court abandoned the eighth (mandatory OSG) item in 2003 -- over CJP's dissent that the OSG's 'active intervention was necessary,' like the Church's 'defensor vinculi,' to prevent the process from 'degenerat[ing] to a divorce fiat' -- and in Te v. Te (2009) and Azcueta (2009) held the guidelines should not be a 'straightjacket,' directing courts to decide 'on a case-to-case basis.' The result, CJP warns, is that there are 'no more firm standards,' outcomes are hard to predict, and defective judgments often go unappealed because the OSG is no longer bound to defend the marriage -- so critics say the country is 'back to the most liberal divorce procedure in the world,' the 'Pinoy edition' of absolute divorce.
